label: rem:qstar-decay-sector-q0
title: The $S = 0$ point $q^{*}$ is conditional on $c_3^{\mathrm{even}} = -\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)$, not an independent determination of $q_0$
html:
The bar-odd decay observable, taken here in its c_3-level normalization S(q) = c_3(q) + \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) (the same object as the preceding remark's \mathfrak{Q}_\beta/E_0 up to the ladder rescaling), is a deterministic function of the substrate modulus: c_3(q) is the ladder extractor c_3 = (\mathfrak{Q}_\beta / Q_{N2} - 1)/u^3, where Q_{N2} is the c_2-level ladder truncation of \mathfrak{Q}_\beta, u = b\,\hbar_q^2, and \mathfrak{Q}_\beta, m_e are fixed physical constants. Its zero is therefore root-found, not interpolated from anchors:

  q^{*} \approx 1.10997859303152\ldots,

the point where c_3 = -\mathrm{Vol}(4_1) exactly — the pure bar-even substrate point with vanishing decay projection (\varepsilon = \mathrm{Im}(q) = 0 in the reading of the interpreted conjecture's candidate (iii)). It lies \approx 80.3\% of the way from the proton anchor toward the muon anchor under the half-argument phase evaluation; see the parameter-sensitivity note below.

q^{*} is independent of both mass-sector pins — it uses neither m_\mathfrak{p} nor m_\mu — but it is not an independent third determination of q_0. Such a claim would be circular: q^{*} is defined above as the root of S(q) = c_3(q) + \mathrm{Vol}(4_1), so locating it presupposes c_3^{\mathrm{even}} = -\mathrm{Vol}(4_1). It is a determination of q_0 conditional on that hypothesis, which is precisely the hypothesis an independent determination would have to avoid.

The supporting statistics do not rescue it. At q^{*} the muon ratio m_\mu/m_e deviates \approx 42.7 ppb from CODATA, versus \approx 1.4 ppb at the muon anchor and \approx 211 ppb at the proton anchor; and q^{*} is indeed not the statistical reconciliation of the \mu–\mathfrak{p} tension (the precision-weighted mean sits \approx 0.0007\% muon-ward, essentially at the proton anchor, which is \approx 367\times more precise, while q^{*} sits 80.3\% muon-ward). Both remain true and neither is evidence, because the 80.3\% is a reading of \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)'s own value: every constant V in the window (-c_3(\mu), -c_3(\mathfrak{p})) = (2.0202,\, 2.0693) of width 0.0491 places a zero between the anchors, and as V sweeps that window the corresponding q^{*}_V sweeps the entire anchor interval. \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) = 2.0299 sits 80.30\% of the way from the proton end of that window, the same figure. Choosing a different in-window constant relocates q^{*} and would produce a different percentage, equally far from both pins and from their weighted mean.

The \mu–\mathfrak{p} substrate tension is therefore two-way, holding between the two mass pins alone.

Parameter sensitivity. The placement of q^{*} between the anchors depends on the weight z entering the phase \alpha = (z-1)h/2 of the c_3 extractor. Setting z = 1/(\sqrt{q} + 1/\sqrt{q}) \approx 0.49932 gives \alpha \approx -0.052336, whereas the canonical Markov parameter z = q^3/(q^2+1) \approx 0.61269 gives \alpha \approx -0.040486, a 23\% shift. Root-finding the same extractor with only z changed yields:

parameter z q^{*} position
1/(\sqrt{q} + 1/\sqrt{q}) 1.10997859340\ldots inside the anchor interval
q^3/(q^2+1) 1.11023370740\ldots outside it, by \approx 19{,}921 anchor-gaps

The anchor interval is only 1.281 \times 10^{-8} wide, and substituting z = q^3/(q^2+1) displaces q^{*} by 2.55 \times 10^{-4}.

Two consequences follow. First, the 80.3\% placement is specific to z = 1/(\sqrt{q} + 1/\sqrt{q}) and does not carry over to z = q^3/(q^2+1), where re-deriving the c_3 ladder is separate work. Second, the skeptical conclusion of this remark is unaffected, and is strengthened: the 80.3\% is a reading of \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)'s own value rather than independent evidence, and at z = q^3/(q^2+1) the root falls outside the anchor interval altogether. The exclusion argument is likewise untouched: its root-monotonicity and root-uniqueness statements concern an abstract \Phi assumed strictly monotone on the anchor interval without reference to z or \alpha, and the numerical premise holds for both parameters (\Phi(q^{*}) \approx -3.606 at z = q^3/(q^2+1) versus -3.631 at z = 1/(\sqrt{q} + 1/\sqrt{q}) — nonzero and of the same sign).

The residual empirical content must be stated with its error bar, because the error bar dominates it. The extractor amplifies the experimental \mathfrak{Q}_\beta uncertainty by 1/u^3, giving \sigma(c_3) = \sigma(\mathfrak{Q}_\beta)/(Q_{N2}u^3) \approx \pm 1.262 — about 61\% of |c_3|. Against that band, c_3's proximity to -\mathrm{Vol}(4_1) is 0.031\sigma at the proton anchor and 0.008\sigma at the muon anchor. These are not close agreements in the evidential sense; they are the absence of a measurement, since every candidate constant in [0.807,\, 3.331] agrees at least as well. That interval is 51\times wider than the 0.049 genericity window quoted above, so the window understates the ambiguity by that factor. Distinguishing \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) from a generic in-band constant requires a neutron Q-value sharper by \approx 32\times (proton) or \approx 130\times (muon).

The same arithmetic denies the converse: 0.031\sigma is no evidence against a 4_1-volume ingredient either. Whether the identification is structural remains the open question of Physical role of \mathrm{Im}(q), which this remark interprets; it is settled neither by q^{*} nor by the present precision.

Two calibrating facts sharpen how q^{*} may be used. First, the famous hypersensitivity dc_3/dq \approx 4.7 \times 10^{6} is not a singularity of the underlying object: S'(q^{*}) \approx 2.37 \times (1/u^3), a smooth O(1) prefactor magnified by the 1/u^3 ladder inversion. Second, the precision of q^{*} is limited by the experimental neutron Q-value, dq^{*}/d\mathfrak{Q}_\beta \approx -0.539. A sharper \mathfrak{Q}_\beta measurement directly sharpens q^{*}, a concrete falsifiable lever that additional mass anchors at the same \mathfrak{Q}_\beta would not provide.
